chapters.html:
"Take care of yourself, you’ve got long journey ahead," Hieronymus said, pulling his son into one last embrace.  

"We’ll throw a huge party when you come back,” Audata added, holding on tightly, reluctant to let go. “And if you make any friends, bring them home.”

"Or a boyfriend." Cyrene chimed in with a smirk, never missing a chance to tease Phainon.

"Cyrene!" Phainon’s cheeks flushed pink. “I’m going to Castrum Kremnos to train! Not to-"

"Doesn’t mean you can’t meet the love of your life,” she cut him off, wrapping her arms around him in a tight hug. “You better write to us,” she added, letting the vulnerability slip in her voice

Though she tried to hide it, she was sad to watch him leave. Phainon had always been her closest friend, more like a brother than anything else. They’d been inseparable since childhood. But Phainon had a dream, to train in Castrum Kremnos and learn their ways of battle.

"I will," he promised, pulling away.

"Goodbye everyone. I'll be back soon." Phainon waved goodbye, forcing himself to turn before he could change his mind. The road ahead was uncertain. He was leaving behind everything he knew, but he wasn’t afraid. He was ready.

The journey took days, but at last, he arrived.

Castrum Kremnos, land of strife and warriors. Renowned for its formidable fighters, it attracted countless outsiders eager to learn their combat techniques. To accommodate this interest, the prince’s advisors had established a program to ensure visitors experienced the full depth of Kremnoan training and culture.

From what Phainon understood, once a year the gates were opened to foreigners wishing to learn the art of battle. Anyone could join, regardless of origin, age, or gender. Beyond that, Phainon had no idea what to expect.

Phainon found himself in a wide, open courtyard surrounded by crumbling pillars and scorched training dummies. About fifty others were already gathered. He struck up a conversation with a group of guys who had met on their way there, as well as two young girls who had apparently run away from home. There was even a kid, no older than ten.

Their conversation was abruptly cut short when a voice sliced through the chatter, loud and sharp.

"Welcome to Castrum Kremnos. I am Leonnius, one of the prince’s advisors."

The man, Leonnius, stood tall on a raised stone platform. He was slender but powerful-looking, with strong looking legs, short hair, and a large scar that ran across his face. Behind him stood several guards in traditional Kremnoan armor.

"You’ve all come here with a goal in mind," he continued, his voice commanding. "But I’m here to tell you, it won’t be as easy as you think. Here, you’ll learn the way of the Kremnoan blade, and that means following our rules. If that displeases you, you’re free to leave now, having learned nothing."

Silence fell over the crowd. Phainon knew what he had signed up for, but he wasn’t sure the others did.

"My fellow generals and I will begin your training tomorrow. Tonight, you rest." With that, Leonnius turned and walked away.

Phainon and the others were then led to their sleeping quarters. Each room housed around twenty-five people.

"It’s so cramped in here," Phainon muttered, scanning the room for an empty bed.

“Not for long,” someone beside him said with an arrogant laugh. “Half of you won’t last the first day.”

Phainon didn’t reply. He just dropped his bag by a bed and sat down, staring at the wall across from him. Something told him it was going to be a short night. Best to get whatever rest he could while he still had the chance.

Raised in Aedes Elysiae, Phainon’s body was conditioned to rise with the sun, often before it. Every morning at five, he had helped his father in the fields before the heat set in. It proved to be a useful habit, because only minutes after he woke up, armored men barged into the room, barking commands at full volume.

“Wake up, you lazy fools! You have ten minutes to get dressed and make it to the dining hall, or say goodbye to breakfast!”

Chaos erupted. Some people tumbled out of bed, others curled up and tried to block out the noise. Phainon was already moving. While others scrambled, he was pulling on his clothes. He was the first to step out of the room, earning an approving nod from the lead guard.

Soon, others joined Phainon as they were led to the dining hall. There, they were each handed a cup of strange green liquid, along with a piece of bread, a slice of cheese, and a single egg.

A man stood at the front, overseeing them. He looked different from the others, no armor, just simple light clothing. His black hair hung to his shoulders, and while his build lacked the usual Kremnoan bulk, his eyes held a sharpness.

“This is where you’ll be taking all your meals,” he announced. “The prince values nutrition, so lunch and dinner will be more filling. Breakfast, however, must be light, your training demands it.”

“And I suggest you all drink my concoction if you want to avoid sore limbs tomorrow,” he added with a smile that bordered on threatening. He seemed knowledgeable in medicine. Phainon didn’t hesitate, he downed the mixture in one go. It was bitter, but not unbearable.

Training that day was brutal. Leonnius, the man who had welcomed them the day before, was now in charge, and he wasn't going easy on them. They were forced to run for an hour, swing wooden swords hundreds of times, and push a boulder across the plains until their bodies gave out.

Phainon collapsed at the finish line before anyone else, drenched in sweat and gasping for air.

“Get up, pretty boy. Training hasn’t even started,” Leonnius said, offering him a flask of water.

“What?” Phainon wheezed, chugging the water. No wonder people quit on the first day. He gave the general a grateful nod.

“Combat training begins as soon as the others finish pushing their boulders,” Leonnius said, eyeing Phainon with interest. “You’ve got potential.”

That one remark was all Phainon needed. Somehow, a compliment from a handsome general was enough to reignite his fire and carry him through the rest of the training.

At least, that’s what he liked to think, because the moment hand-to-hand combat began, Phainon realized he was doomed. He was up against Kremnoans who had been fighting with their bare hands their entire lives. He couldn’t remember the last time he’d lost this badly.

After each defeat, his opponent would offer him a hand.

“Are you tired yet?” he’d ask, grinning.

Phainon would grit his teeth, swallow the pain, shake his head, and force himself back into a fighting stance.

By lunchtime, Phainon was thoroughly beaten. The dining tables were half empty. He couldn’t tell if the missing recruits had quit or if they were in the infirmary. He did notice a white tent in the corner of the training grounds.

“Good job to everyone who’s still standing,” Leonnius announced, his voice dripping with sarcasm. “Your performances today were pathetic, but that’s why you’re here.” He chuckled, scanning their exhausted faces. “Training’s done for the day, but your work isn’t. After lunch, go make yourselves useful. Help in the forge, the kitchen, anywhere you're needed. Just don’t sit around. There’s always work to be done.”

With that, the general turned and left.

Helping out was Phainon’s specialty, so he looked forward to the task.

After a hearty and delicious meal, he wandered the camp to see where he might lend a hand. Most of the other trainees had already snagged the easier jobs like cleaning weapons and chopping vegetables for dinner. So Phainon turned his attention to the white tent. Maybe they could use an extra hand in there.

As soon as Phainon stepped into the tent, he was greeted by the sight of two fellow trainees lying on beds, getting patched up by the man who had spoken to them that morning. Phainon realized he still didn’t know the man’s name.

“Are you here to get patched up? Give me a minute, and I’ll be right with you,” the man said, his tone gentler than it had been earlier.

“Actually, I’m here to ask if you need any help,” Phainon replied, feeling a little awkward.

“Oh, of course. Could you start by cutting some bandages?””

Phainon got to work without hesitation. He cut bandages, helped grind a soothing balm for pain relief, and even learned how to clean minor wounds properly. Once things settled down, the man gave him a warm smile.

“Your help was appreciated. Most recruits avoid the infirmary like the plague.”

“It’s no problem at all. I just wanted to make myself useful.”

“May I ask your name?”

“I’m Phainon, from Aedes Elysiae. Sorry, I didn’t catch your name this morning.”

“My bad, I didn’t introduce myself. I’m Perdikkas, one of the prince’s advisors.”

Phainon blinked. First Leonnius, now Perdikkas. Apparently, the prince had a talent for surrounding himself with ridiculously good-looking men. He couldn't help but wonder, was the prince just as handsome, or was he a hideous man compensating by surrounding himself with beauty?

As they talked, Perdikkas was mixing herbs into a bowl, grinding them with ease.

“Are those the same herbs used to make the drink from this morning?” Phainon asked, wrinkling his nose.

“They are. How’d you know?”

“The smell gave it away.” Phainon made a face, and Perdikkas chuckled.

“Trust me, the taste and smell are awful, but tomorrow, you’ll thank me. You’ll barely feel any soreness.”

They eventually parted ways, with Phainon promising to return and help again as long as he remained here. While he made his way to the dining hall reserved for trainees, Perdikkas headed toward the prince’s quarters, where the inner circle of advisors and other Kremnoan fighters had already gathered. Mydeimos was known to consider meals to be a sacred time, meant to be spent with comrades and loved ones.

Mydei was seated at the head of a long table, pouring goat milk into a cup already halfway filled with pomegranate juice. Around him sat Hephaestion, Leonnius, Ptolemy, and Peucesta, talking, laughing, enjoying the company.

“I swear, Mydei, if you ruin another cup of fresh pomegranate juice with goat milk…”

“I’m not ruining it. You just lack the taste to appreciate it.”

“Are you two seriously arguing about this again?” Perdikkas asked, slipping into his seat. His presence immediately drew the group’s attention.

“Where were you?” Leonnius asked. “Did that many recruits end up in the infirmary? I swear we went easy on them today.”

“Not at all,” Perdikkas replied. “I just got caught up talking to one of them. He’s more charming than most of the foreigners we usually get.” He began serving himself food as he spoke.

“Was it the white haired one? What was his name again?”

“Phainon. Yes, him.”

“Is he promising?” Mydeimos asked, more engaged than usual. He rarely paid attention to the recruit program, but something about this one seemed to pique his interest.

“I think he’ll make a fine fighter, once we sharpen him a bit,” Leonnius said with pride, as though Phainon were already his personal project.

Hephaestion raised an eyebrow. “Where is he from?”

“Aedes Elysiae,” Perdikkas replied.

“That’s a long way off,” Ptolemy whistled, clearly impressed. “Try not to break him, Leonnius.”

Peucesta, who had been quietly enjoying his meal, finally chimed in. “If he’s come this far and still has fight in him, he won’t break. That kind of grit doesn’t show up often.”

Mydeimos gave a slight nod, still swirling his drink. “I’m curious to see if he lasts. Most don’t make it past the third day.”

“He hasn’t broken yet,” Perdikkas said, glancing over at the prince. “He even offered to help in the infirmary without being asked. You don’t see that very often.”

Hephaestion leaned back with a smirk, eyes narrowing at Perdikkas. “You sound impressed. Should we be expecting a new favorite?”

Perdikkas rolled his eyes. “Don’t start.”

Mydeimos finally took a sip of his drink. “Maybe I’ll meet him myself. If he lasts a month.”

That quieted the table for a moment. When Mydei showed interest in someone, it was never casual. Every man at that table knew it well. Once, they had each been in that same position.

Perdikkas exchanged a knowing glance with Hephaestion before returning to his food.

Leonnius chuckled. “Well, now he really has to survive. Poor guy.”

Phainon woke up the next day and slipped back into the same grueling training. But this time, he noticed something different. Leonnius was putting more pressure on him than anyone else. He was made to run longer, push heavier boulders, and during hand-to-hand combat, he was thrown against opponents twice his size. He couldn’t even beat the ones his own size, how was he supposed to survive this?

“I think Leonnius wants me to quit,” Phainon muttered as Perdikkas dabbed the blood from under his nose. Luckily, it wasn’t broken, just bruised after taking a punch from a man whose fist was bigger than his entire face.

“What makes you think that?” Perdikkas asked, focused on cleaning the wound.

“He’s making things harder for me. But only me!” Phainon winced as the disinfectant stung.

“Is it working?” Perdikkas asked, keeping his tone light but avoiding eye contact. After yesterday’s conversation, he was genuinely curious.

“It’s pissing me off,” Phainon admitted. “But no. I wouldn’t quit because of that. It makes me want to succeed even more.”

Perdikkas had to suppress a smile. “Then he’s doing his job. Leonnius only pushes the ones he thinks are worth the effort. He wouldn’t give you more than he believes you can handle.”

Once Phainon was bandaged up, he thanked Perdikkas and was sent off to rest in his room for the remainder of the day.

But just as Phainon was about to collapse onto his bed, something caught his eye. A small envelope was resting neatly on the sheets. Its pink edges and bow sealing it were all too familiar. He didn’t even need to open it to know who it was from.

“Dear Phainon,

Did you make it to Castrum Kremnos? What’s it like there? And how are they treating you?

We’re all worried about you, so I hope you're enjoying your stay. It’s so calm here without you. I can finally read my books in peace without you pestering me every five minutes.

But in all seriousness, we all miss you. And we’re hoping to hear from you soon.

-Cyrene.”

Phainon smiled, letting out a bittersweet chuckle. Leave it to Cyrene to make him feel even more homesick than he already was. He needed to write back, but didn’t have any paper with him. Maybe he’ll ask Perdikkas about it tomorrow.

On the third day, Phainon was surprised to see that only ten trainees remained out of the original fifty. He wasn’t sure if he was finally getting used to the intensity, or if the extra rest from the previous night had done the trick, but training didn’t feel as impossible as it had before.

By the end of the day, he wasn’t completely drained. For once, he had the energy to focus during hand-to-hand combat. And for the first time since arriving, he could see his opponent’s movements, anticipate their attack patterns, and dodge with intention instead of desperation.

Phainon faced off against a man twice his size. He punched relentlessly but Phainon was able to discern a pattern. Before long he slipped through the barrage of attacks, finding an opening and punching him straight in the face, sending him down.

For a split second, silence reigned on the training grounds.

Then Leonnius, who had been watching from the sidelines, let out a satisfied huff.

Phainon extended a hand to help his opponent up, still processing what had happened.

“Well done, boy,” the man said, accepting the gesture with a grin. “You’re stronger than you look.”

That was one thing Phainon admired about the Kremnoans, their respect in defeat, and the spirit they brought into every fight.

Of course, his celebration was short-lived. His next few opponents humbled him fast, knocking him to the ground. He had a long way to go. Years of sword training had made him agile, but bare-handed combat was still foreign territory.

From a spot near the edge of the training grounds, Hephaestion had been watching with his arms crossed. As Phainon got knocked down once again by another opponent, he turned to Leonnius, who approached with a smirk.

“Well?” Leonnius asked, proud of his trainee. “Did you see it?”

Hephaestion shrugged. “All I saw was a lucky punch.”

“Not willing to admit he has potential?” Leonnius smirked.

“He got defeated in the next three matches,” Hephaestion pointed out. “He has spirit, I’ll give him that. But heart alone doesn’t win battles.”

“I’m not saying he’s ready,” Leonnius sighed. “But he’s worth watching. He learns and he wants it more than anyone else here.”

Hephaestion didn’t respond. He looked out over the field again, watching Phainon pick himself up off the floor for the fourth time that morning. This was the boy Leonnius had hope in? That country boy was supposed to catch up to someone like Mydei?

It was insulting.

He didn’t understand what Leonnius was so impressed by, and he certainly didn’t want to see the prince’s hopes raised for nothing.

Later that day, Phainon met up with Perdikkas in the infirmary, as had become their routine.

“I heard about your little accomplishment,” Perdikkas said as he sorted through medicines.

Phainon looked up from where he was crushing leaves for yet another one of Perdikkas’ strange remedies. “How do you always know everything when you’re locked up in here all day?”

“A bird told me,” Perdikkas replied. And by bird, he meant Leonnius, who had talked his ear off earlier, ranting about Phainon’s progress and Hephaestion not seeing the potential.

Phainon didn’t bother pressing further. He knew better by now.

“Do you know where I can get paper?” He asked instead

“For what?”

“I want to write a letter to my family,” Phainon said, dusting off his hands.

“The library has what you need. We can go together when we’re done here. I need to return a book anyway.”

When they finally wrapped up their tasks, Perdikkas guided Phainon through a foreign corridor, fancier and cleaner than the ones the trainee got to see every day. They eventually reached the tall wooden doors of the library, carved with intricate patterns.

Rows upon rows of books stretched into the dim, golden lit space. Shelves towered above them, packed with books. Cozy reading areas were scattered throughout, some with simple desks, others with deep couches that looked perfect for a cozy read. The light was soft, perfect for reading but easy on the eyes.

Perdikkas led Phainon to a secluded corner, which contained single tables with individual lights. At the corner were boxes of supply to write letters.

“When you’re done, put your letter in that box,” Perdikkas explained. “It gets emptied at the end of the week and sent out.”

Then, giving Phainon a small nod, he stepped away to return his book, leaving him alone. Phainon sat down, unfolded a sheet of paper, and began writing his reply to Cyrene.

“Dear Cyrene,

Your letter made me homesick. I hope you’re proud of yourself.

The training is difficult, but I’m pulling through. The food is good, and I’ve already made a friend.”

He paused, hesitating for a moment. Were he and Perdikkas friends? He hoped so. They got along well enough, and Perdikkas didn’t seem to mind his company. That had to count for something. With a shrug, he continued writing, adding a few sentimental lines, asking her to greet his parents for him, and assuring her he was doing well.

Once finished, he sealed the envelope, wrote the address on the back and slipped it into the box.

As he turned to leave, he heard faint voices whispering. He recognized one of them instantly.

Rounding the corner, he spotted Perdikkas seated on a couch, speaking to two men with books in hand. The man on the right was tall and broad-shouldered, with blonde hair and a golden laurel tucked into his curls. He looked like a statue come to life, yet Phainon barely spared him a second glance, because the man beside him stole his breath away.

He was shirtless. Why was he shirtless? His sculpted torso on full display, adorned with red tattoos that spiraled across his chest, down his arms and legs. Even his face was marked with red. Phainon couldn’t tell if it was ink or makeup. His hair was shoulder-length, fading from blonde into red, a single braid falling over one side. Golden jewelry glinted on his ears, neck, and arms, studded with blue gems that caught the light.

Phainon was floored. Stunned. His jaw practically hit the floor.

Then the man looked up. Their eyes met, and Phainon felt his soul leave his body.

“But… if there’s a chance in the next life, you should come visit my library.”

Where had that thought come from? He had no idea. Probably his brain trying to protect itself from a catastrophic gay panic. He barely noticed Perdikkas speaking to him.

“Are you done?” Perdikkas asked.

“Yeah… all done.”

“Great. Let’s go.” Perdikkas stood and turned back to the two men. “See you two at dinner.”

Phainon followed reluctantly, his eyes trailing behind them one last time. Though he didn’t realize that the tattooed man, still lounging on the couch, had been watching him just as intently the entire time.

Once they were out of sight, the man’s gaze lingered on the corner where Phainon had disappeared.

“Mydei, darling,” Ptolemy said, flipping a page in his book without looking up, “you’re being as subtle as a droma in the marketplace.”

“Is this the white haired foreigner Leonnius was talking about?” Mydei asked, not bothering to respond to Ptolemy’s jab.

“I believe so,” Ptolemy replied, watching Mydei out of the corner of his eye.

Mydei fell silent. His gaze dropped back to the open book in his hands, though his mind was clearly elsewhere. He might have to visit Leonnius’ training grounds one of these days.

Meanwhile, Phainon was still buzzing with questions, no idea who the tattooed man was or even his name. Maybe he was another one of the prince’s advisors. After all, the prince seemed to have a habit of surrounding himself with beauties. The other man with him was good-looking too, so that seemed like a fair guess.

“Phainon, I can practically hear you thinking,” Perdikkas said, clearly amused.

“What do I have to do to know who he is?” Phainon asked, too desperate to feel any shame.

“Which one are you talking about?” Perdikkas asked innocently, though his smirk gave him away.

“Don’t do this to me…”

“You’re easy to tease,” Perdikkas chuckled. “You were just ogling the crown prince of Castrum Kremnos, Mydeimos.”

Phainon’s jaw nearly hit the floor, for the second time that evening. He had convinced himself the prince had to be ugly. He hadn’t even considered this possibility.

“Nice. Good to know I have absolutely zero chance,” Phainon muttered, defeated. Better to get his heart broken early than risk getting his hopes up.

Perdikkas only laughed softly. Knowing Mydei, Phainon probably had the best chance of anyone he’d ever met. But he wasn’t going to tell him that. Not yet.

Weeks passed, and Phainon was getting better. He was adjusting to the harsh routine. The warm-ups that once left him drained were now child’s play. He fought Kremnoans one after another with ease, taking them down like it was nothing. Occasionally, he’d meet a strong opponent and lose, but he always demanded a rematch the next day, and almost always came out victorious.

Mydei, having just finished his own training, decided to swing by Leonnius’ training grounds. He stayed far enough not to be seen.

The way Phainon moved, how he blocked, parried, and attacked was impressive. Not enough to stand against him, of course, but still… something about him was intriguing.

“They’re making a big deal about him,” said a voice behind Mydei. He didn’t have to turn to recognize Hephaestion. “I don’t see it.”

“How about we end his training with Leonnius and put him with you?” Mydei suggested casually.

“What?? Mydei, you’ve got to be kidding me.”

Hephaestion wasn’t having it, but he also knew, deep down, that he could never say no to Mydei.

“Your training is harsher than Leonnius’, and it’s about time the country boy learned how to properly wield a weapon, don’t you think?”

Hephaestion sighed. He really didn’t have a choice in the matter. “He’s reckless and undisciplined. If I hand him a weapon he’ll end up dead.”

“Exactly, and that’s why I want you to sharpen him” Mydei said, stepping away.

Hephaestion studied him for a moment. “You like him.”

Mydei was silent for a moment before saying, “Is that so bad?”

Hephaestion sighed again in resignation. “Fine. But don’t come after me if I break him.”

That afternoon, Phainon and Perdikkas were quietly tidying up the infirmary after a busier day than usual. Apparently, some monsters had attacked without warning, catching many off guard. Perdikkas was exhausted and deeply grateful for Phainon’s help.

The comfortable silence between them was broken when Leonnius stepped into the tent.

“Is Phainon here?” he asked, peeking inside.

Phainon looked up from the stack of bloodied bandages he was getting rid of.

“I’m here,” he said, wiping his hands on a rag. “What’s going on?”

Leonnius stepped fully inside, arms crossed, his expression unreadable.

“I wanted to speak with you,” he began. “About your training.”

Perdikkas looked up from where he was organizing a row of vials, then glanced at Phainon. He stayed quiet but didn’t leave, sensing it wasn’t a private conversation.

Leonnius didn’t seem to mind. He walked over to an empty bed, sitting down, looking uncharacteristically thoughtful.

“As of tomorrow, you’ll no longer be training under me.”

The words hit harder than Phainon expected. He looked confused. “Wait… what? Did I mess up?”

Leonnius gave a short laugh, shaking his head. “No. You didn’t mess up. If anything, you’ve exceeded expectations.”

He leaned forward slightly, elbows on his knees. “You’ve worked hard. You pushed through every challenge I threw at you, and you’ve done it without complaining. You’ve earned my respect.”

Perdikkas shot Phainon a brief, proud look but stayed quiet, giving them space.

“Then… why stop?” Phainon asked, confused.

“Because someone higher up noticed you. And they want to take over your training.” Leonnius let that hang for a moment before adding, “Hephaestion.”

Phainon blinked. “You’re kidding.”

“Do I look like I’m kidding?” Leonnius raised an eyebrow. “He specifically requested you. That doesn’t happen often.”

Has Phainon met Hephaestion? No. But did he need to meet him to know he was the fiercest fighter among the Kremnoans after Mydeimos? Also no.

Phainon opened his mouth, then closed it again. “He’s going to kill me.”

Leonnius chuckled. “He might try. But if you can handle it, and I think you can, you’ll be a force to be reckoned with.”

Silence fell between them for a moment.

Perdikkas finally spoke, his voice calming. “That’s an honor, you know. Getting picked by Hephaestion. Terrifying, but impressive.”

Phainon exhaled slowly, still processing. “I’ll miss training with you.”

Leonnius stood, placing a hand on Phainon’s shoulder. “You’ve got something special. Don’t let him crush it out of you.”

“I’ll try.”

Leonnius gave him a nod, then turned and left the tent.

A moment passed.

Phainon groaned. “I’m going to die.”

Perdikkas chuckled lightly. “Well, you know where to find me if you need to be taken care of.”

The following day, Phainon woke up, got dressed, had breakfast, and headed to the training grounds with everyone else, just like usual. Except this time, he didn’t stop at the plains. Instead, he climbed the hill beyond them, walking for several minutes before reaching the top. There, scattered across the field, stood a group of men wearing traditional Kremnoan armor, their movements precise and disciplined.

It didn’t take him long to spot Hephaestion.

As expected from one of the prince’s trusted advisors, he was stunning. Long blond hair, piercing green eyes, and an authority that radiated from him despite his scrawny figure. Phainon had heard the rumors of people underestimated Hephaestion all the time, until they saw him fight. On the battlefield, he was a relentless force.

When their eyes met, Hephaestion didn’t speak. He simply turned and motioned for Phainon to follow. They walked in silence to a nearby armory, where rows of weapons were stacked neatly.

“Pick one,” Hephaestion said, stopping in front of the racks. “And just so we’re clear, you’re not leaving this field until you’ve mastered it. Even if it kills you.”

Off to a great start.

But Phainon didn’t hesitate. When it came to weapons, he already knew what he’d choose. He’d spent most of his childhood training with a sword, it had always felt like an extension of himself.

He tested a few from the rack. Some were too light, others too heavy. Then, his hand closed around one that felt… right. The hilt was smooth, well-balanced, and carved with a sun emblem. It felt like it had been waiting for him.

“I’m choosing this one,” Phainon said, holding it up.

Hephaestion studied him for a moment, then nodded.

“Then let’s see what you’ve got.”

Mydei and his advisors were all impatiently waiting in the dining room for Hephaestion to finally show up.

“I swear, if he kills Phainon, I’m going to-” Leonnius muttered, tapping his foot against the floor.

“I strongly advise you don’t finish that sentence,” Peucesta interrupted, not even looking up from his drink. “You couldn’t beat Hephaestion at anything.”

“Maybe I should’ve stayed in the infirmary,” Perdikkas mumbled, fidgeting with a spoon he’d picked up. “Just in case.”

“What’s with you two?” Ptolemy sighed, annoyed. “Phainon can’t possibly be that charming that you're both worrying yourselves to death.” He didn’t dare look at Mydei, who, despite never having met Phainon properly, was already down bad.

“You’d be surprised,” Perdikkas said with a small smile.

Footsteps echoed down the corridor, unmistakably Hephaestion’s. The room fell into silence. Hephaestion groaned as soon as he saw them all staring at him. “Don’t start or I’ll have lunch elsewhere,” he warned, striding over to his seat.

“Oh, come on!” Leonnius exclaimed, throwing his hands in the air.

“Does he at least need medical assistance?” Perdikkas asked, half-joking half not.

Hephaestion looked like he wasn’t going to answer. But then he caught the expecting look in Mydei’s eyes.

He sighed.

“There’s nothing for me to teach him,” Hephaestion muttered, and dug into his food.

Leonnius and Perdikkas exchanged confused glances.

But Mydei understood. He smiled faintly and picked up his fork.

After lunch, Perdikkas and Leonnius practically sprinted to the infirmary.

There, to their surprise, they found Phainon already at work, wrapping a bandage around a soldier’s bruised arm. He finished tying it off, gave the man a nod, and watched him leave. The moment the soldier was gone, Leonnius pulled Phainon into a tight hug.

“You’re alive!”

Phainon, caught off guard, let out a huff and laughed, returning the hug. “You guys seriously overreacted. I thought Hephaestion was going to kill me, but training with him isn’t that bad!”

“What did you even do?” Perdikkas asked, tugging Phainon away from Leonnius.

“He made me pick a weapon. Then we warmed up, and I had to spar with a few people. After I beat them, he fought me himself.”

“And?” Leonnius asked impatiently.

“And what?”

“Who won?” Both of them demanded.

“I did,” Phainon said like it was nothing. “But I think he was holding back. I mean, I heard he’s supposed to be the second strongest here, but honestly? I didn’t have a hard time.”

Perdikkas and Leonnius exchanged a look of disbelief. Hephaestion never held back. It didn’t matter if it was a recruit or Mydeimos himself. He fought with everything he’s got.

But this didn’t make sense. Phainon had only just started training, so how could he have reached that level so quickly?

“Phainon, have you ever trained with a weapon before?” Perdikkas asked.

“Yeah! I used to train with the sword every day back home.” Phainon smiled, reminiscing of old times.

That explained everything. Leonnius had honed his body and sharpened his reflexes, but the skill had always been there. All Phainon needed was a weapon in his hand and a worthy opponent to awaken it.

“Did Hephaestion say anything to you after you were done?” Leonnius asked.

“No, he just said training was over for the day and walked off.”

“Wow.” Perdikkas raised an eyebrow. “It’s not every day someone finishes a spar with Hephaestion without a scratch. I don’t even see a bruise on you.”

“Actually…” Phainon lifted the side of his shirt, revealing a dark bruise spreading across his side. “I think I might’ve broken a rib or two…”

Perdikkas’ eyes widened. “Phainon!” He immediately pushed him down onto one of the empty beds. “And you’re telling us now? After letting Leonnius crush you in a hug?”

He hurried to a drawer and began rummaging for his tools.

“It doesn’t even hurt that much,” Phainon protested, only to wince as Perdikkas began pressing gently around the bruise.

“Uh-huh. Sure it doesn’t.” Perdikkas gave him a flat look. “Fortunately, nothing’s broken. Just badly bruised. But I’m putting you on mandatory rest tomorrow.”

Phainon groaned. “Seriously?”

“Yes. Doctor’s orders.” Perdikkas crossed his arms.

Leonnius chuckled. “Look on the bright side, you survived Hephaestion and you get a day off. That’s a win if you ask me.”

“What am I even supposed to do on a day off?” Phainon muttered, flinching slightly as Perdikkas applied a cold balm to his bruise.

“Go visit the library,” Perdikkas suggested, smirking. “With a little luck, you might bump into the prince. Who knows where that could lead?”

“Stop teasing me…” Phainon groaned, covering his face with one hand.

“Am I missing something?” Leonnius asked, glancing between them.

“Phainon thinks Mydei’s hot,” Perdikkas said.

Leonnius shrugged. “Don’t we all?”

After Phainon was patched up and sitting comfortably, he finally asked a question that had been nagging at him for days.

“Did the prince choose all his advisors to be hot on purpose?”

Perdikkas blinked. “What?”

“I’m serious!” Phainon said. “I mean, look at you guys.”

Perdikkas rubbed his temples. “Did Hephaestion hit your head too?”

Leonnius smirked. “So… you think I’m hot?”

Phainon groaned. “This is why I didn’t want to say anything.”

“Oh, no. You opened this door.” Leonnius teased, clearly enjoying himself.

Perdikkas rolled his eyes. “Great. Now you’ve inflated his ego. There’s no going back.”

“He got you pretty good, huh?” Mydei stepped into Hephaestion’s quarters, walking over to where the blonde man sat.

“How many times do I have to ask you to knock?” Hephaestion sighed. “Mind your manners, prince.” There was no bite in his voice, just weary affection. He was awkwardly wrapping bandages around his torso, making a poor job of it.

“Let me do it,” Mydei said, gently taking the bandages from him. He began unwrapping and redoing them properly, careful not to hurt him. “Why didn’t you go to Perdikkas?”

Hephaestion ignored the question and looked Mydei in the eyes. “I was skeptical about this country boy. Thought Leonnius was exaggerating. But after testing him myself... I think he might be the one.”

A small smile tugged at Mydei’s lips as he finished securing the bandage. “It’s not like you to doubt people.”

“You deserve the best, Mydeimos. And if I can’t be that for you, then at the very least, I want to help find the one who is.”

Mydei paused, then pulled Hephaestion into a soft embrace. “You’ll always be by my side. You’re my dearest friend.”

Hephaestion closed his eyes, letting himself rest against Mydei for just a moment longer.

Yes... but that’s all I’ll ever be, he thought, the words aching in his chest.

Chapter Notes

This was supposed to be a 10k words fic at best, but Mydei and Phainon keep getting distracted. I wasn't going to upload this until i came back from my trip but I got impatient so here you go!
Anyway here's some more fluff and enjoy!

Despite it being his day off, Phainon didn’t get to sleep in. His body woke him up just as early as always, and no matter how hard he tried, he couldn’t fall back asleep. With a sigh, he sat up. The room was quiet, he was alone.

He reached under the bed and pulled out the sword he had chosen, admiring the way the morning light shined along the blade. It had surprised him when they told him he could keep it, even in his room. Still, he wasn’t about to argue. Somehow, having it nearby brought him comfort.

There was no reason to visit the library. Cyrene hadn’t written back yet, and he was far too restless to spend the day buried in books. Instead, he made his way toward a quiet field he’d noticed during training. No one ever seemed to be there, and the overgrown greenery reminded him of the wheat fields back in Aedes Elysiae.

It was peaceful. The only sounds were the distant screams from the training grounds and the clash of weapons. But when he focused a bit more, he picked up on something else, another sound coming from a different direction.

They say curiosity kills the cat, but Phainon had always been compared more to a puppy, so he figured he’d be fine.

He followed the sound through a narrow path until it opened into another training ground. This one made of smooth concrete, with tall stone pillars encircling the space like a temple. In the center stood Mydei, crimson crystals flying around him as he launched one flaming strike after another into the air, each one more precise than the last.

Phainon stood frozen at the edge, eyes fixed on him.

Unlike the loose robe he wore at the library, today Mydei was dressed in something more fitting for combat, though "armor" might be the wrong term. Most of his torso was still bare, his tattoos glowing with each attack he launched out. But at least he wore pants.

Phainon swallowed hard. This was fine. He certainly wasn’t turned on by the sight. Absolutely not.

Unfortunately, fate wasn’t on his side, because at that exact moment, Mydei turned around, sensing he was being watched, and their eyes met.

Mydei lowered his hand, the red crystals fading into as he tilted his head slightly. “Enjoying the view?” he called, smirk on his face.

“I was just… walking,” Phainon blurted. “This field looked... empty.”

Great Phainon. Good job, making a fool out of yourself.

Mydei hummed, clearly amused. “Come closer, country boy. If you’re going to spy, at least do it properly.”

Phainon wasn’t sure if he was about to pass out or combust, but either way, his legs moved before his brain caught up.

“Aren’t you supposed to be resting today?” Mydei asked, watching him approach.

Phainon blinked. “How do you know that?”

He hadn’t even realized the prince knew who he was.

“You’re all my advisors seem to be talking about lately. Phainon did this, Phainon said that,” Mydei said with a sigh. “Perdikkas was especially adamant about keeping you off the training grounds today.”

“He’s overreacting. I’m completely fine,” Phainon replied. Which wasn’t a total lie. Sure, his side was still bruised, but the pain was manageable.

Mydei gave him a knowing smirk. “Then I assume you wouldn’t mind a short sparring session.”

For a second, Phainon just stared, wondering if he’d heard that right. Was he seriously being challenged to spar with the prince?

“Unless you’re too scared to face me,” Mydei added with a grin, enjoying himself.

That was all it took to spark Phainon’s competitive side. “Absolutely not! I’m ready.”

He straightened, grateful he'd thought to bring his sword with him.

They stood on opposite ends of the training grounds. Before Phainon could even register it, Mydei had already closed the distance, charging at him. The prince was fierce, relentless in his assault, each strike painting the area red. Phainon had no choice but to stay on the defensive, blocking and dodging as best he could.

But little by little, he began to see a pattern. Mydei was fast, unpredictable, but not untouchable. Once Phainon adjusted to the rhythm, he stepped back, recalibrated, and finally went on the offensive.

He didn’t know how long they sparred. Minutes? Hours? At some point, they’d drawn an audience, but Phainon didn’t let that distract him. He was too focused. No matter how many times Mydei knocked him down or sent him flying into a pillar, Phainon always got back up. And each time he did, Mydei laughed, and smiled at him like he was having the time of his life.

It fueled Phainon more than any victory could.

Mydei was radiant. Whether under the golden rays of morning sunshine or the silver light of moonlight, he glowed with a kind of beauty that made it hard to look away. Phainon couldn’t stop watching him, didn’t want to.

Eventually, his body gave out. As much as he wanted to keep going, to push further just to see Mydei let loose again, his strength had run dry. In one final attempt, he launched a desperate attack that sent both of them tumbling to the ground, Phainon landing on top of the prince.

They both panted, chests heaving. Mydei let out a breathless laugh and gave Phainon a half-hearted shove, rolling him off.

“Not bad…” Mydei laughed, voice hoarse but amused.

Phainon let his head fall back against the ground, smiling despite the ache in his limbs. “I could say the same to you…”

Phainon didn’t register anything after that. The moment the words left his mouth, he passed out.

When he woke up again, he wasn’t on the training grounds, and this definitely wasn’t his room. The faint scent of herbs gave it away before his eyes fully adjusted to the light. He was in the infirmary.

He tried to sit up, but immediately winced as pain shot through his body. Every muscle screamed in protest, reminding him of every hit, and every moment he had refused to give up.

Turning his head, he saw Perdikkas slumped in a chair beside the bed, fast asleep, his head resting against the mattress near Phainon’s arm. His brows furrowed even in sleep, as if still worrying.

Phainon’s chest tightened with guilt. He hadn't meant to make anyone worry. Especially not Perdikkas. Sparring with the prince had felt like a dream, like stepping into a different world. But now, seeing Perdikkas here, exhaustion etched on his face, reality hit.

“I really need to stop causing trouble,” Phainon muttered to himself.

Perdikkas stirred at the sound, blinking awake. The moment he registered Phainon sitting up, he shot upright.

“You’re awake,” he said, relief in his voice, then narrowed his eyes. “What were you thinking?”

Phainon offered a sheepish smile. “That I could handle it?”

Perdikkas sighed, rubbing his temples like he was holding back a lecture. “Do you even know how long you two sparred?”

“I wasn’t exactly checking the time…”

“Ten days and ten nights.”

Phainon stared at him. “You’re joking.”

“I wish I were,” Perdikkas said. “You both passed out on the tenth night.”

Phainon was dumbfounded. Ten days? He’d thought it was a few hours, maybe a full day at most, but days?

“I hope you realize what that means,” Perdikkas added.

“That I’ll get to spar with him more often?”

“No! Well, yes, probably, but that’s not the point. The point is, you and Mydei are now seen as equals.”

Phainon’s brain stalled. That thought hadn’t even occurred to him. “Wait, no one’s ever managed a draw against the prince before?”

Perdikkas shook his head. “Never.”

“Not even Hephaestion?”

“The longest they ever went was three days. Mydei still won.”

Phainon sank back into the mattress, stunned. Equal to Mydei? It felt surreal. He was honored, yes, but if anyone asked how he managed it, he wasn’t sure he could say the truth. That it wasn’t the thrill of battle that drove him, it was Mydei’s smile. That look he gave him mid-fight. Phainon would’ve fought another ten days just to see it again.

The tent flap rustled, and Leonnius stepped in, his grin wide the second he saw Phainon.

“Our sleeping beauty is finally awake,” he said, eyeing Perdikkas cautiously before adding, “I’d hug you, but someone’s banned me from touching you until further notice.”

Perdikkas shot him a glare. “It’s a miracle his bones aren’t shattered. We don’t need you to finish the job.”

Leonnius raised his arms in defeat before eyeing Phainon. “You slept for so long. A while longer and we were gonna try a true love’s kiss,” he added with a wink.

“Wait, how long was I out?” Phainon asked.

“Three days,” Perdikkas replied, standing to gather some herbs and medicine.

Phainon’s eyes widened. “Three days?? Did the prince wake up yet…?”

Leonnius nodded. “Yeah. Morning after you collapsed.”

Phainon groaned, throwing his head back dramatically. “Damn it… that means I lost.”

Perdikkas gave him a look like he was this close to smacking him. “Is this a competition to you?”

“Well, yeah,” Phainon said, completely serious. “We didn’t finish the fight, so whoever stayed unconscious longer technically lost.”

“Don’t overthink it, Mydei has the curse of immortality. He heals faster than most people. Doesn’t mean you actually lost.” Leonnius reassured him.

“Still feels like it.” Phainon mumbled.

Leonnius leaned in. “You’re the only person who’s ever pushed him that far. That’s gotta count for something.”

It did. Maybe more than anything Phainon had ever accomplished.

Mydei had spent the entire day helping with repairs to the training grounds he and Phainon had destroyed. As prince, he could’ve easily left the work to others, but a sense of responsibility compelled him to take part.

That evening, he was scheduled to have dinner with his mother. Gorgo, queen of Castrum Kremnos, was a busy woman, and their moments together were few and far between since the death of his father. Mydei suspected there was more to the sudden invitation than just a family meal, but he chose to wait and let her bring it up.

Once his work was done, he cleaned up and made his way to the private dining room where she awaited him.

The dining room was quiet, lit by the golden flicker of candlelight. Gorgo sat at the head of the table, her posture firm but her gaze soft.

“You’re late,” she said, though her tone was more affectionate than scolding.

“I was helping with repairs,” Mydei replied, taking the seat across from her.

“So you do take responsibility for your actions.” She arched an eyebrow.

He chuckled. “You’re not that surprised.”

“No,” she admitted. “I suppose I’m not.”

They ate in comfortable silence for a few moments. Gorgo stirred her wine before glancing up at him.

“So. Ten days and ten nights.”

Mydei paused, his fork midway to his mouth.

“It’s quite the feat, Mydeimos. No one’s ever lasted more than three days against you. Not even Hephaestion.”

He set down his fork. “It didn’t feel like ten days.”

“No, it wouldn’t. Not when you’re completely enthralled.”

He shot her a warning look. “Mother.”

“What?” she said, feigning innocence. “I’m just saying, it reminded me of your father and I when we first met.”

Mydei blinked. “Seriously?”

“Oh yes,” she said with a wistful smile. “We dueled for ten days, too. By the tenth night, he dropped his sword and asked me to be queen of Castrum Kremnos.”

“You’ve never told me that.”

“You never asked.” She leaned in, resting her chin on her hand. “So… when’s your proposal?”

Mydei huffed and leaned back, arms crossing over his chest. “Please. We barely know each other.”

“Then maybe it’s time you changed that.” Gorgo returned to her meal, her smile lingering.

Mydei fell silent.

Yes… maybe it is time.

If Phainon is awake tomorrow, he’ll make his move.

The next day, Phainon was under strict orders not to leave the infirmary. Perdikkas had gone out to the market to stock up on supplies, leaving Phainon alone with a bottle of some foul smelling purple liquid and a threat.

“This bottle better be empty by the time I get back,” Perdikkas had threatened.

Phainon didn’t dare disobey him, but seriously, the stuff was vile. Bitter enough to make his entire mouth shrivel. He tried sipping it slowly, wincing after every swallow. Maybe he could ask Leonnius to sneak him something sweet later, anything to get the taste out of his mouth.

Wrapped in what felt like a ridiculous number of bandages, Phainon laid in bed, aching from head to toe. He was convinced half of the bandages were just Perdikkas being dramatic. Still, he couldn't move much even if he wanted to.

But more than anything else, he missed Mydei.

He’d seen that smile for ten days straight, heard his laugh, watched him, felt his touch, despite it being rough. Phainon was convinced that if he saw Mydei again, he’d heal twice as fast.

He was lost in thought when the tent’s flap rustled.

Phainon glanced up, expecting Leonnius, or maybe even Perdikkas, back early to scold him, but instead, in stepped Mydei.

Out of his combat gear, Mydei wore a simple white robe that left half his chest bare and exposed most of his legs. Phainon did his best not to let his eyes wander to those thighs, the very same ones that had nearly crushed his head during their sparring match. If he had died back then, it would've been a blissful way to go.

But now, with Mydei right in front of him, Phainon was struggling to understand why he was even here.

“Prince?” he asked, trying to sound composed.

“We fought for ten days,” Mydei said, settling into the chair beside him. “You’ve earned the right to call me by my name.”

Phainon blinked, then nodded. “Sorry, Mydei. What are you doing here?”

“Checking up on the damage I caused,” Mydei said, holding up a covered plate, “and bringing you this. I figured Perdikkas probably left you with some horrible medicine.”

Curious, Phainon lifted the cover, and immediately his face lit up. A small stack of golden and warm honeycakes greeted him.

“Wow. These smell incredible.”

“I wasn’t sure how sweet you like them,” Mydei added, gesturing to a tiny jar of syrup tucked beside the plate. “So I brought extra, just in case.”

“Wait… you made these yourself?”

“Of course I did. Any decent warrior should know how to cook something basic.”

“These aren’t basic,” Phainon said, picking one up and taking a bite. He hummed.  “This is amazing.”

“Hm…” Mydei hummed, eyeing Phainon in a way no one ever had. It wasn’t subtle, and it certainly wasn’t innocent. Phainon wasn’t sure what to make of it, only that it made his skin feel hot.

“If only you weren’t wrapped in bandages.”

Phainon flushed. “That’s Perdikkas being overprotective. I don’t need that many.”

“I don’t know,” Mydei said with a teasing smile, his gaze drifting down the length of Phainon’s body. Was he checking him out? Phainon’s breath hitched. Great, he looked half dead while Mydei sat there in a robe that barely covered anything, his chest and legs completely healed and unfairly exposed, as if he was showing off.

“Would you dare going against Perdikkas’ orders?” Mydei asked, challenging him.

Phainon raised a brow. “If it were for something important…”

“Like what?” Mydei leaned in, eyes fixed on him.

Phainon swallowed. “What are you offering?”

Mydei’s smirk widened. “That depends on how brave you’re feeling right now.”

Silence fell between them. Phainon’s fingers clenched slightly in the bedsheets, heart thudding in his chest. He couldn’t quite tell if this was still teasing, or if things were about to escalate. Either way, he wasn’t about to back down.

“I think I can handle you.” He said, his voice lower.

That drew a light chuckle from Mydei. “Careful, country boy. If you say things like that, I might start getting ideas.”

“Then maybe you should start acting on those ideas.”

They stayed like that for a moment longer, staring at each other across the infirmary bed, both unwilling to be the first to look away.

Until they heard voices approaching.

“…and he tried to scam me. Can you believe that?” Came Perdikkas’ voice.

“Trying to scam you of all people was a poor choice,” Leonnius replied, walking into the infirmary.

Phainon and Mydei both straightened at once, too quickly. The sudden motion made Phainon dizzy, but he would never admit it.

“Oh, Mydei, you’re here!” Leonnius said with a smile, stepping inside with a few boxes in his arms. He set them down on the nearby table. Perdikkas followed close behind, carrying a couple of small bags.

“Not for long,” Mydei said. “I was just checking on Phainon, but I should get going.”

“Already?” Phainon asked, sounding far too much like a sad puppy. A complete contrast to how he was acting a few seconds ago.

“Feel free to visit the training grounds again,” Mydei said, then caught the look Perdikkas was giving him. “Once you get the doctor’s approval, of course.”

Perdikkas nodded in and Phainon pouted. He knew he was in no shape to spar with Mydei, but he didn’t want to let go yet.

As Mydei stepped out, silence lingered for a beat too long.

Then Leonnius turned, eyebrow raised and smirking. “Well, that wasn’t suspicious at all.”

“I don’t know what you’re talking about,” Phainon said, sitting up a little straighter, only to regret it when his ribs protested.

“Oh, come on,” Leonnius grinned, leaning against the edge of the bed. “He made you honeycakes. Did we ever mention that Mydei’s love language is food?”

Phainon looked down at the empty plate in his lap. “Maybe he was just being nice.”

“Nice, my ass. He looked at you like he wanted to devour you.”

Phainon groaned, covering his face with one hand.

Perdikkas, who had been unpacking one of the bags, finally turned around, with a smirk himself. “While I do agree with what Leonnius said, I would advise you to restrain yourself, should you wish to keep your internal organs intact.”

Phainon looked at him confused.

Leonnius snorted. “He means don’t try to make out with him before you can walk again.”

“I wasn’t planning to,” Phainon protested, his face now burning. “Can we not talk about this?”

“Oh no,” Perdikkas said, clearly amused. “We are absolutely going to talk about this. With the way you two were looking at each other, I feel obligated to ensure you don’t cross any lines before you’re in full health.”

“Besides,” Leonnius added, arms crossed and smirking, “this is the most exciting thing to happen in Castrum Kremnos in months. Don’t ruin it for us.”

“I wasn’t going to kiss him,” Phainon muttered.

“But you wanted to,” Leonnius teased, nudging him with a raised brow.

“Maybe… but it’s intimidating! What if I mess it up?”

“Mess up kissing?” Perdikkas rolled his eyes. “You sound like a teenager who’s never had their first kiss.”

Silence.

Both Perdikkas and Leonnius turned to look at him.

“…Don’t tell me,” Leonnius said, already grinning.

Phainon’s face turned bright red. “Shut up! Aedes Elysiae is a tiny village! Everyone knows each other, so it’s not exactly a romantic setting!”

Leonnius burst into a fit of laughter, nearly doubling over, while Perdikkas tried, unsuccessfully, to hide his amusement behind a cough.

“Nikador help him,” Leonnius laughed, wiping a tear from his eye. “Your first kiss might actually be with Mydei. This is better than I ever imagined.”

“Stop laughing at my misery,” Phainon groaned, burying his face in his hands. “I’m going to die in this bed, and it’ll be your fault.”

“If you need to practice,” Perdikkas chimed in, “Leonnius would surely volunteer, as an apology.”

Phainon lifted his head just enough to glare. “No thanks. I’d rather embarrass myself with Mydei than kiss him.”

“Hey!” Leonnius said, looking offended. “I’ll have you know I’m an excellent kisser. I’ve received many praises.”

“From who, your reflection?” Phainon shot back.

Leonnius smirked. “From Mydei, actually.”

Phainon blinked. “I’m sorry, what?”

“Stop tormenting him,” Perdikkas said, crossing his arms. “We’ve all kissed Mydei at some point. Leonnius isn’t special.”

“What??” Phainon looked between them, utterly bewildered. “Is that some kind of tradition or… what do you mean you’ve all kissed him?”

Leonnius shrugged, far too pleased with himself. “It just kind of happens when you grow up around him. We were all horny teenagers once.”

“Yeah, but why always him?” Phainon asked, looking vaguely betrayed.

“Everyone has a crush on him when they first meet him.” Perdikkas explained.

Phainon leaned back against the pillows, completely shocked. “So I’m not special?”

“No, you are,” Leonnius said, more serious now. “Mydei’s usually a lot more direct. But with you, he’s taking his time. That means something.”

“You can think of it like he’s courting you. He’s being serious.” Perdikkas added.

Phainon sighed, unsure whether that made things better or worse.

Things changed significantly once Phainon was finally allowed to leave the infirmary.

First, he was given his own private room. No more sleeping in the room with the other trainees. When he arrived, he discovered that all of his belongings had already been moved. Not that he had much, just a few spare sets of clothes and his sword.

The room itself was spacious, more than he ever expected. A large bed in the center, looking like the most comfortable thing he’d ever laid eyes on. The wide window overlooked a field of tall grass, gently swaying in the breeze, reminding him of the wheat fields of his hometown.

There was even a desk, and on it, he found two pink envelopes. Letters from Cyrene, he guessed.

He opened the older one first. It was a simple letter, checking in, updating him on home, how everyone was doing. But the second one, the more recent, was much more frantic.

“Dear Phainon,

You haven’t answered my last letter in two weeks. I’m worried about you. I don’t know if it got lost, or if you’re too busy to reply, but everyone is asking. I hope this one finds you. Please write back and let us know you’re okay.

-Cyrene”

Phainon felt guilty. He hadn’t meant to ignore her. But after the ten-day fight, he’d slept for three days straight, then spent another five recovering under Perdikkas’ constant supervision. He hadn’t even known he was getting letters.

He’d go to the library tonight. Send something back to reassure her.

Once he finished settling into his new space, Phainon grabbed his sword and headed for the training grounds.

It was his first time seeing the renovations. The arena was smooth and reinforced, the damage from his battle with Mydei erased. It still felt a little surreal, being declared Mydei’s equal. From now on, he wouldn’t train with Leonnius or Hephaestion. His sessions would be with Mydei directly.

That said, he’d be using a wooden sword, and Mydei would be restricted from using his powers, unless they were ready for another ten-day spar.

Mydei was already there, stretching. Thankfully, he was in his fighting outfit. No robe. Phainon wouldn’t have to battle the distraction of bare thighs. Though, the half-open chest was still a problem. Self-restraint, apparently, was part of the training now.

“Took you long enough to recover,” Mydei called with a smirk once he spotted him.

“I was good to go by the second day,” Phainon replied, stepping into the circle and picking up the wooden sword laid out for him. It matched his real one in weight and balance. “Perdikkas was just being overprotective.”

“He asked me not to go too hard on you,” Mydei said as he shifted into a fighting stance. “But I don’t think I’ll listen.”

“You don’t have to,” Phainon replied, matching his posture.

He was ready for the first strike, whenever it came.

Mydei lunged first, as expected.

Phainon barely blocked in time, the wooden sword clashing with the gauntlet in a heavy crack. The shock ran through his arms, but he held his ground, pivoting to the side. Mydei was faster than he remembered.

They exchanged blows, each stronger than the other. Phainon had a feeling his sword wouldn’t last, the wood chips falling from the cracks.

Phainon went for a feint, Mydei saw through it instantly and spun behind him. Before Phainon could react, Mydei’s leg knocked his balance out from under him, and the next thing he knew, his back hit the ground with a hard thud. A gasp escaped him when Mydei straddled his waist in one fluid motion, pinning both of Phainon’s wrists to the floor with his hands.

“You really thought that feint would work?” Mydei asked, smug.

Phainon stared up at him, breathless, not from the fight, but from the sight. Mydei’s hair hung slightly forward, blonde strands catching the sunlight. His chest rose and fell above him, exposed, sweat glistening on his collarbones.

He was close. Too close.

“I had to try something,” Phainon muttered, struggling slightly under the hold, but not really trying to get away. He was enjoying himself far too much.

“Are you going to surrender?” Mydei leaned in a little more.

Phainon narrowed his eyes. “Not yet.”

With a sudden twist, Phainon yanked one arm free, using the momentum to flip them. Mydei let out a surprised grunt as he hit the ground, and now it was Phainon who straddled him, gripping Mydei’s wrists and pressing him to the floor.

Mydei blinked up at him, stunned, but then his lips shaped into a smirk.

Phainon had to admit, being pinned down was nice, but pinning Mydei was something else entirely. From this angle, he could see everything under a new light. Mydei looked good like this, his powerful body, momentarily at Phainon’s mercy. Mydei shifted beneath him, trying to wriggle free.

“Not a chance.” Phainon tightened his grip and adjusted his weight, locking Mydei’s hips in place with his thighs. The movement earned him a short, surprised breath from the prince, almost a laugh, almost something else.

“Do you surrender?” Phainon asked, smirking.

“In your dreams,” Mydei shot back, his voice low as he struggled under the hold.

Their faces were close. Phainon could feel the warmth of Mydei’s breath. If he just leaned in a little closer...

His thoughts slipped for a second too long, and in one swift motion, Mydei snapped forward and head-butted him, throwing him off balance. Phainon let out a startled grunt, falling back just as Mydei surged upward and flipped their positions again.

Before he could react, Mydei straddled him and wrapped his gauntlet against Phainon’s neck, not tight, just enough to make him unable to move.

“Were this a real battle,” Mydei said, smirking down at him, “you’d be dead.”

But Phainon wasn’t listening. He was too busy staring up at Mydei again, heart pounding in his chest, for reasons that had nothing to do with losing.

“You were distracted. That’s why you lost,” Mydei said as he stood, offering a hand.

Phainon took it, letting himself be pulled up. “Yeah… I let my thoughts wander,” he admitted, brushing dirt off his clothes.

“Well,” Mydei said, turning away, “next time your thoughts stray during battle… do something about it. You might not get a second chance.”

Phainon watched him. “What’s that supposed to mean?”

Mydei didn’t look back. He simply grabbed a cloth from the edge of the circle and started wiping sweat off his neck. “It means hesitation gets you killed. Or worse, gets someone else killed.”

That wasn’t all he meant. Phainon could feel it. The way Mydei’s voice had lowered, the weight in his words.

“Is that what happened to you?” Phainon asked quietly. “You hesitated once?”

Mydei paused, still turned away. “Something like that.”

Silence stretched between them.

Mydei would never forget the day his own father turned against him. How he’d pointed his spear at the man who raised him, and hesitated, just for a second. A second too long. His father had seen the opening, ready to strike… and Gorgo had stepped between them. She took the blow meant for her son.

For a moment, he thought she was gone. But she survived, because she was Gorgo. She wouldn’t go down so easily. Since that day, Mydei had sworn never to hesitate again.

Phainon took a step closer, his voice softer now. “I don’t want to hesitate.”

This time, Mydei glanced over his shoulder, his expression was unreadable, but something had shifted. “Then stop thinking, and start acting. Especially if it’s something you want.”

Their eyes locked. Neither moved.

It felt different this time. Mydei was letting his guard down. There was something fragile in the way he looked at Phainon, but it didn’t make him feel weak.

Phainon opened his mouth, unsure what would come out, only knowing he wanted to say something.

“Mydei and Phainon, sitting in a tree!” Leonnius’ voice rang out across the field, ruining the moment.

Mydei’s jaw tensed as he let out an exasperated sigh. “What do you want, Leonnius?”

“Krateros is looking for you,” Leonnius called as he approached. “Said something about interrogating captured soldiers. Also, he’s in a terrible mood, so good luck.”

Mydei groaned, rubbing his temple. “He always is.”

Then, turning back to Phainon with a more composed look, he added, “Same time tomorrow?”

Phainon smiled. “Wouldn’t miss it.”

As Mydei walked off, Phainon stood there a moment longer. He brought a hand to his chest, pressing lightly over his heart. It was still beating too fast.

Leonnius sidled up beside him. “You gonna kiss him next time or keep staring at his mouth like that?”

Phainon gave him a flat look. “Do you ever stop talking?”

“Nope,” Leonnius grinned, clapping him on the back. “But if you don’t make a move soon, I’m starting a betting pool.”

Phainon rolled his eyes but couldn't help the small smile tugging at his lips.

Despite not having to help out anymore, Phainon kept visiting Perdikkas at the infirmary to lend a hand. It gave him something to do and he enjoyed Perdikkas’ company. Afterward, later in the evening, he made his way to the library alone.

He gathered what he needed, paper, ink, a seal, and was about to settle into a quiet corner to write when curiosity tugged at him. His eyes drifted toward the far end of the library, to the secluded reading corner where he’d first seen Mydei.

Would he be there again?

Phainon walked through the tall shelves, until he rounded the corner. The comfortable couch was there, but it was empty.

He let out a quiet sigh, amused at himself for even expecting it. He turned to leave, when…

“Looking for someone?”

Phainon jumped slightly, turning to find Mydei leaning against one of the bookcases behind him. In one hand, he held a book with a worn leather cover. He wore that damn robe again, barely tied, chest and legs exposed. It couldn’t be allowed in a library! Or Phainon was just a pervert who couldn’t keep his eyes in check.

“You could give someone a heart attack!” Phainon said, trying and failing to keep his eyes on Mydei’s face.

“Someone?” Mydei asked, stepping closer. “Or just you?”

He brushed past Phainon and sank into the couch. He opened the book on his lap and leaned back, robe parting just enough to make Phainon immediately regret not maintaining eye contact.

“You planning to just stand there staring,” Mydei asked without looking up, “or are you going to sit down?”

Phainon hesitated, then slowly stepped forward and sat on the second couch, the single-seat one. Mydei clicked his tongue, finally glancing up from his book with a look of exaggerated disappointment.

“Seriously? Are you dense on purpose?”

Phainon reddened. “What?”

“You walk all the way here, clearly hoping to run into me, and then you go sit over there like I’ve got the plague.”

Phainon crossed his arms. “I wasn’t hoping to run into you.”

“You came to this corner of the library,” Mydei said flatly, “the least practical place to write a letter. The lighting is too warm, there’s no proper desk, and there are pillows everywhere. You weren’t looking for a desk. You were looking for me.”

“I was just…” Phainon faltered. “I thought maybe you’d be here.”

Mydei smirked. “Which proves my point. Now stop being difficult and come sit here. I don’t bite.”

Phainon relented, and sat beside Mydei this time, close, but not too close. The couch was wide enough that they weren’t touching, but Phainon was very aware of how little space there was between them.

Mydei turned a page in his book and spoke again, “Who’s the letter for?”

“My friend. Her name is Cyrene.” Phainon fidgeted with the corner of the paper. “I didn’t know she’d sent anything until today. I feel bad for not replying sooner.”

“Then don’t waste time. Write it now,” Mydei said, returning his attention to his book.

Phainon began writing.

“Dear Cyrene,

I’m sorry it took me so long to reply. So much has happened, and I only just saw your letters today. I wish I could explain everything, but I don’t even know where to begin. Maybe I can come back to Aedes Elysiae soon and tell you all about it in person.”

Beside him, Mydei leaned his head back against the couch, watching Phainon from the corner of his eye. He didn’t try to read the letter, he wasn’t here to invade privacy. But still, he was growing tired of pretending they weren’t drawn to each other. So, he leaned in and gently rested his head on Phainon’s shoulder.

“Wha-”

“Can you still write?” Mydei asked calmly, eyes flicking to the page.

Phainon swallowed. “Y-yeah.”

“Then don’t mind me,” Mydei said, turning back to his book.

Phainon tried to refocus on the letter, heart pounding. Mydei's hair brushed against his neck, and his skin felt warm. He’d written four words before he stilled again.

This won’t do. He wanted Mydei closer, now that they’ve touched.  He reached up and gently cradled the back of Mydei’s head, guiding him down and sideways until Mydei’s head was resting comfortably in his lap. Mydei let him, one brow raised in surprise, but he didn’t resist. Instead, he curled slightly on the couch, book still in hand, spine relaxed.

“That’s better,” Phainon said under his breath, almost to himself, as he brushed a few strands of hair from Mydei’s forehead.

“Hmm,” Mydei hummed, shifting just enough to look up at him from where he laid. “Comfortable now?”

Phainon chuckled softly. “Yeah. Are you?”

Mydei nodded. “But you can’t write with me in your lap.”

“It can wait,” Phainon said, his gaze lingering. He couldn’t help it, he really liked looking at Mydei from this angle. The way his hair fell gently to the side, and the way his eyes locked with his own, like there was no one else in the world. His heart pounded so hard he was almost certain Mydei could hear it.

They held the moment, eyes locked, comfortable silence stretching.

Then, Mydei spoke. “Tell me about Aedes Elysiae.”

The question caught Phainon off guard, but he didn’t hesitate. Any chance to talk about home was welcome.

“It’s beautiful,” he said, the fondness already showing on his face. “Covered in wheat fields, flowers, and trees. You can smell the ocean from anywhere in the village.”

Mydei listened without interrupting, his eyes never leaving Phainon’s.

“Everyone knows everyone. It gets busy, especially during harvest season. I used to sit in the wheat fields every sunset whenever I needed alone time. Everything turns golden for a few minutes, like the whole world’s glowing.”

A faint smile tugged at Mydei’s lips. “You talk about it like it’s a dream.”

Phainon looked down at him. “Sometimes it feels like one. Especially here.”

Mydei reached up lazily, his fingers brushing along the side of Phainon’s jaw. “Take me there.”

Phainon’s breath caught, pulse quickening, if that was even possible. “Are you serious?”

“Hm…” Mydei hummed. “I want to see the place that makes you smile like that.”

“I’d like that,” Phainon said, voice low.

“I’ll make the necessary arrangements so we can leave as soon as possible,” Mydei added, as if it were already decided.

Phainon took Mydei’s hand gently, guiding it away from his jaw. He brought it to his lips, pressing a soft, lingering kiss into the center of Mydei’s palm. “I just know you’ll love it.”

“I don’t doubt it,” Mydei murmured, watching him closely. He sat up, finding himself at Phainon’s eye level now despite the awkward way they were sitting.

Without a word, Phainon shifted and lifted Mydei easily into his lap, settling him there like it was the most natural thing in the world. His hands stayed on Mydei’s waist, his fingers gently holding the exposed skin.

He remembered Mydei’s words from earlier.

“Then stop thinking, and start acting. Especially if it’s something you want.”

So, for once, Phainon didn’t hesitate.

He raised his hands, cradling Mydei’s face gently between his palms. Their eyes met, and then Phainon leaned in and kissed him.

He was careful at first, almost unsure, like he still couldn’t believe it was happening. But Mydei responded, leaning into the kiss, his arms sliding around Phainon’s neck to pull him closer.

When they finally broke apart, Mydei stayed close, lips hovering near his, as if he was already considering kissing him again.

“You’re not bad,” he murmured, eyes half-lidded and mouth curved in a teasing smile.

Phainon was a little dazed. “Thanks? That was… actually my first kiss.”

Mydei froze, then leaned back just enough to stare at him. “Your first?”

“Please don’t make a big deal out of it…” Phainon’s cheeks reddened. Perdikkas and Leonnius had teased him enough about it already.

“Then I guess you’ll have to shut me up,” Mydei said.

Phainon didn’t need to be told twice. He leaned in again, capturing Mydei’s lips in his own, less hesitant this time. Mydei welcomed it with a hum, his fingers curling into the fabric of Phainon’s shirt, pulling him closer.

If Phainon had any doubts about whether he was doing it right, Mydei’s response erased them.

“I’m starving…” Leonnius groaned, flopping dramatically into his seat.

“Where’s Mydei? He’s always here first,” Hephaestion asked, crossing his arms as he scanned the empty spot at the table.

Ptolemy entered just then, settling into his usual place. “Don’t bother waiting. Let’s just eat without him.”

Peucesta raised an eyebrow. “Since when do we eat without Mydei?”

“He’s not coming,” Ptolemy said, annoyed. “He’s too busy making out with his lover boy.”

That earned a few surprised looks.

“Oh?” Perdikkas smirked, clearly too entertained. “Well, well… Looks like someone owes me a drink.”

Leonnius groaned and dropped his head against the table. “Unbelievable. I really thought Phainon would chicken out.”

Hephaestion blinked. “Wait, you two made a bet on whether they’d kiss?”

“Yup. I said it would happen within the week. Leonnius said no way.” Perdikkas said.

“In my defense,” Leonnius muttered, “I didn’t think he had it in him.”

“Why didn’t you tell us?” Peucesta chuckled, sipping from his cup. “I wanted in on the bet.”

Ptolemy, still looked annoyed, having seen it all in the library. “You want to bet now? How about who’s sitting in whose lap?”

Leonnius groaned. “Please. That’s not even worth betting on. Phainon’s definitely folded into Mydei’s lap like a love-struck puppy.”

“That’s where you’re wrong,” Ptolemy said.

Silence fell across the table.

“…What?” Peucesta looked confused.

Perdikkas laughed. “I knew Mydei had it bad, but not that bad.”
