Chapter Notes

First of all I'm sorry it took so long to post chapter 3! I usually write my fics on my phone's note app then edit everything on my laptop. But i got a new phone and I accidentally deleted the first draft of this chapter. So it took a while to rewrite all of it.
But I hope you'll enjoy this chapter regardless!

Warning: The beginning of this chapter contains suggestive content but the rest of it will be tame.

Phainon had never kissed anyone before Mydei, but now that he knew what it felt like, he wasn’t sure he could ever stop. Mydei's lips tasted faintly sweet, like pomegranate, addictive in a way that made his head spin. Their bodies pressed close, tangled together on the couch, and every touch sent a shiver down his spine.

His hand slid from Mydei’s waist to his shoulder, where the robe was held together by a metal clasp. His fingers toyed with it, hesitating for only a second before slipping beneath it. When he pushed it aside, the fabric gave way easily, falling off Mydei’s shoulder and pooling loosely around his waist.

Now, Phainon had full access to Mydei’s back. It was surreal, having Mydei like this, kissing him, touching him. His fingers traced the line of his shoulder, drifting down to his back. When he touched lower, pressing in gentle circles, Mydei let out a sound that nearly made Phainon melt.

He needed to hear it again.

He pressed in a little deeper, drawing slow circles with his fingers.

“You’re rather bold for someone who claims to be inexperienced,” Mydei murmured, voice slightly breathless.

Phainon didn’t even try to deny it. “You’re irresistible,” he whispered, already leaning in for another kiss.

But then, the sharp sound of books tumbling to the ground jolted them both. Instinctively, Phainon pushed Mydei back, almost knocking him off his lap. He immediately regretted it when he saw the look of annoyance on Mydei’s face, very much displeased at being interrupted.

When they turned toward the source of the noise, they found Ptolemy crouched nearby, calmly collecting the fallen books.

“My bad. Didn’t mean to interrupt... that.” He said dryly, not even trying to hide the sarcasm as he turned on his heel to leave.

Phainon’s heart dropped to his stomach. Right. They had been making out in a public library. Where anyone could walk in. And now that the haze of desire was lifting, he became painfully aware of how little Mydei was wearing. The prince’s robe had slipped dangerously low on his hips, barely concealing anything.

Meanwhile, Phainon was still fully dressed, flushed, sweaty, and aching in all the worst ways.

Mydei cleared his throat, adjusting his robe. He stood, avoiding Phainon’s gaze.

“I think that’s enough for today,” he said, his voice steady, like nothing had happened.

“Right…” Phainon replied, trying not to sound disappointed. He wasn’t going to beg Mydei to stay. He had dignity... somewhere.

“I’ll see you tomorrow for training.”

“Yeah. Tomorrow.” He repeated, hoping it would fill the silence. Mydei walked off, Ptolemy falling in step beside him. Phainon watched them go, his stomach twisting.

He ran both hands down his face and slumped back on the couch.

“Pull yourself together…” he muttered to himself. His eyes fell on the paper he’d meant to write on earlier.

Right. The letter to Cyrene.

He picked up the pen, trying to focus. Trying not to imagine what might’ve happened if Ptolemy didn’t show up.

Phainon’s brain was blank.

After everything that had just happened, the only sentence he managed to add to the letter was “I’ll be bringing a friend home with me.”

He stared at it. Friend. The word looked strange.

Mydei had said he’d come with him, after all. But… did he mean it like that? Did he see Phainon as just a friend? Definitely not just a friend, Phainon thought, remembering the weight of Mydei’s body in his lap, the taste of his lips, the way he’d hummed when Phainon touched his back.

But still, he didn’t want to misread the situation. Cyrene would never let him live it down if he misunderstood the nature of his relationship with Mydei.

The next day, they met at the training grounds like nothing had happened.

No mention of last night, just Mydei, dressed in full sparring gear. Phainon wasn’t sure if he should feel relieved or disappointed.

“Ready?” Mydei asked, already stretching.

“Yeah,” Phainon replied, rolling his shoulders.

They circled each other, until Mydei lunged without warning, forcing Phainon to scramble to block.

“You’re slow today,” Mydei said mid swing.

“I didn’t sleep much,” Phainon replied, panting. It wasn’t a lie, he’d spent half the night restless in his bed.

“You already forgot what I told you about focus during yesterday’s training?” Mydei asked, lunging again.

“I’m focused,” Phainon grunted. “Just taking my time.”

Mydei narrowed his eyes. “Hm. Sloppy excuse.”

But Phainon was adjusting, learning his rhythm, their bodies falling into a familiar pattern. They were meant to fight side by side, and both of them knew it, how well they read each other's movements, how easily they fell into sync.

Then, with a sudden sidestep, Phainon twisted behind Mydei and pressed him against one of the stone pillars, locking his arm behind his back just enough to keep him still. Mydei let out a sharp breath, surprised. He could have broken free, Phainon knew that, but he didn’t. He stayed.

“Well?” Mydei asked, glancing over his shoulder. “What now?”

Phainon leaned closer, his voice low. “Just checking if I still remember the sensitive spot… right… here.”

His fingers ghosted along Mydei’s back, settling right at a point on his spine, low on his back, exactly where he’d touched the day before, when Mydei had let out that sound.

Mydei inhaled sharply at the contact.

“Thought so,” Phainon murmured, lips curving into a grin. He loved having Mydei at his mercy, it was endearing.

But then Mydei spoke, his voice oddly distant, breaking the flirtatious mood that had set in.

“I’m sure you’ve heard of my immortality curse already.”

Phainon was startled by the sudden shift in tone, wondering where Mydei was going with this. “Yeah?”

“The spot you’re touching, my tenth thoracic vertebrae. That’s my weak spot, and the only way to kill me.”

Phainon froze, hand still resting lightly against Mydei’s back. “What?”

“If there ever comes a day where strife consumes me, and I turn against my people, I want you to be the one to kill me.”

Phainon wanted to protest, to ask why, to refuse. But the tone in Mydei’s voice made it clear, it wasn’t a simple request, but a deep fear. A desperation for someone to anchor him, should he ever lose himself, like he had seen it happen before.

“You got it…” Phainon said after a moment, his voice low. He released his hold on Mydei’s back, holding his hands to turn him around and face him fully. “And you can count on me to have your back. In every way.”

That startled Mydei. For a moment, he looked at Phainon like he wasn’t sure what to say. Then, a faint smile tugged at his lips. The tension in his shoulders eased.

Words were not needed to convey the trust in each other. Phainon raised a hand, brushing a lock of Mydei’s hair behind his ear. His fingers lingered there, tracing his cheek. Mydei leaned into the touch.

Their eyes met, and Mydei closed the distance, pressing his lips softly to Phainon’s. It wasn’t like their previous kiss. This one wasn’t rushed, it was slow, easy. Phainon wrapped an arm protectively around the prince’s back, shielding his weak spot without touching it.

When they finally broke apart, they didn’t speak. Phainon simply rested his forehead against Mydei’s, eyes closed.

“Mydeimos, are you there?”

Krateros’ voice rang out across the training field.

The two broke apart instantly, grateful for the pillar that shielded them from view. Mydei turned around, composed faster than ever, though his slightly flushed cheeks betrayed him.

Krateros approached. “You’re needed. Now.” His tone left no room for protest.

Interruptions weren’t unusual anymore. Perhaps they should start meeting in more private settings.

Mydei likely understood what Krateros was implying. He nodded, then took Phainon’s hand and pressed a kiss to the back of it.

“I’ll see you soon,” he said before departing.

Phainon couldn’t help the small smile creeping onto his face. He probably looked like an idiot, and hadn’t even noticed Krateros still standing there, arms crossed, glaring.

“Ridiculous,” Krateros muttered, catching Phainon’s attention.

“Excuse me?”

“The prince deserves someone of high status at his side, not a love-struck fool,” Krateros said. The words had bite, but Phainon didn’t take them to heart.

“I’m striving to become someone who can proudly stand beside Mydei.”

“His name is Mydeimos. Only his closest allies call him Mydei.”

Well, Krateros clearly hadn’t seen just how close Phainon and Mydei had been behind that pillar a moment ago.

“I’d say we’re pretty close.”

Krateros looked like he might lunge at him any second.

“Watch your tongue,” he snapped before turning and walking away.

That ended more peacefully than Phainon expected. Oh well.

"You’ve got everything you need. Mydei might not need it, but if you get injured, remember how I taught you to-”

“Relax,” Phainon interrupted, stuffing the last of his clothes into the single bag he’d carry over his shoulders. “We’re only leaving for two weeks.”

“The road might be dangerous,” Perdikkas protested, arms crossed across his chest.

“Did you forget how strong Phainon’s gotten since coming here?” Leonnius chimed in from where he laid, sprawled across Phainon’s bed, not bothering to land a hand. “He’ll be fine.”

Perdikkas sighed, clearly unconvinced, but he knew better than to argue further. “Just don’t forget what you’ve learned,” he muttered, turning away.

“I won’t.” Phainon slung the bag over his shoulder and glanced toward the doorway.

Leonnius finally sat up, throwing his arms around Phainon in a sudden hug. “Try not to fall off a cliff or anything.”

“Thanks for the confidence,” Phainon muttered, rolling his eyes, but he hugged him back.

He turned to Perdikkas, who was still facing away, stiff and silent.

“Are you crying?”

“Don’t be ridiculous,” Perdikkas said as he turned around, his eyes unmistakably glossy. “Take care of yourself… and Mydei.”

Phainon almost teared up himself as he pulled Perdikkas into a tight hug. In the time he’d spent here, they’d grown close, closer than he ever expected. And even though they were only supposed to be gone for two weeks, the future was uncertain. There were never guarantees.

“I’ll come back,” Phainon said quietly. “I promise.”

Perdikkas didn’t respond, just gave a nod and held on for a second longer before stepping back.

Phainon offered one last wave to both of them, then turned and left the room, heading toward the gates where Mydei waited.

The moment the door shut behind him, Leonnius flopped back onto the bed with a dramatic sigh.

“You can cry now. He’s gone.”

“I’m not crying, damn it!” Perdikkas snapped, quickly wiping at his eyes. “I was just… getting a bit emotional. I’m gonna miss him, that’s all.”

“Awww,” Leonnius grinned. “You love him.”

“Of course I do,” Perdikkas said with a huff. “Just like I love Mydei. And all of you.”

“How sweet of you,” Leonnius said, hand over his heart.

“Except you. I only like you.”

Leonnius sat up, offended. “Hey! What’s that supposed to mean?”

“That’s what you get for being annoying.”

“You wound me,” Leonnius groaned, flopping back again. “Truly.”

Perdikkas let out a small laugh despite himself, shaking his head. The room already felt quieter without Phainon.

The trip with Mydei felt shorter than the long, lonely journey Phainon had once made alone to Castrum Kremnos. It technically took the same number of days, but this time, the hours slipped by much faster.

They walked along a riverbank, the sound of water peacefully running beside them. The sun was just beginning to dip, and they’d have to set up camp for the night.

“Look how many fish are swimming here,” Phainon said, eyeing the water and the flashes of silver beneath it. “It’d be a crime not to catch some for dinner.”

They’d been living off dried bread and preserved food, practical, but tasteless. The idea of fresh meat made his stomach growl.

“Do you even know how to fish without equipment?” Mydei asked, already setting down his bag.

“I should be the one asking you that, prince.” Phainon gave him a smirk, already kicking off his shoes and rolling up his pants to the knee. He dropped his coat, leaving him in a black short sleeve top.

Mydei huffed, unfastening the top half of his armor. “Prince or not, I am first of all a warrior.”

Phainon turned to the water, determined not to let Mydei’s exposed chest distract him. “We’ll see if that helps you fish.”

They both stood knee deep in the river, eyes locked on the darting fish below. The water was cool, the current gentle.

Just like during their sparring matches, Mydei moved first. With a sudden lunge, he caught a small fish cleanly, holding it up with a smirk.

On the other hand, Phainon crouched lower, focus sharpened. This was something he’d done since he was little. He lunged, coming up with a decently big fish.

Mydei narrowed his eyes.

Without a word, he doubled his efforts, determined not to be outdone. What began as friendly competition slowly escalated, each of them pushing harder. By the time they were done, the sun had dipped completely below the trees, and they were standing in semi-darkness.

“I win!” Phainon declared proudly, holding up his largest catch.

“No, you didn’t,” Mydei countered, stepping out of the river. “I caught more fish than you.”

“But mine are bigger,” Phainon argued, wringing water from the ends of his pants. “They’ll feed us more.”

“Only cooking them will tell,” Mydei replied, already moving to set down their catch.

They got to work without further debate. Phainon gathered dry branches and lit up a fire, while Mydei skinned the fish and skewered them.

Once the fish were cooking, they sat side by side, close to the fire, letting the heat seep into their soaked clothes. But the night was cold.

Phainon tried to act unfazed, arms loosely crossed, but the night air carried a chill, and his soaked pants clung uncomfortably to his legs. He could feel himself trembling, no matter how hard he tried to hide it.

“You’re shaking,” Mydei said, adjusting a skewer that was too close to the fire.

“I’ll be fine once my clothes dry,” Phainon replied, brushing it off. But as if the wind wanted to prove him wrong, a gust swept through, making him shiver.

Without a word, Mydei moved closer, wrapping an arm around Phainon’s shoulders and pulling him into his chest.

“You could’ve just said you were cold,” Mydei said.

“I wasn’t that cold…” Phainon muttered, though he leaned into the warmth almost immediately. Mydei’s body radiated heat. It was unbelievably warm, almost too hot, but Phainon could handle it.

Soon, Mydei reached forward and picked one of the skewers, the fish golden and crisp at the edges.

“This one’s ready,” he said, handing it to Phainon. “You take the first.”

Phainon blinked. “You sure?”

“You’re the one who caught the bigger fish, remember?” Mydei said with a smile. “Might as well enjoy the taste of victory.”

Phainon took the skewer with a smirk. “So you admit it’s my win?”

“Don’t get too cocky,” Mydei replied, mirroring his smirk. “I’ll win our next contest.”

Once the last fish was eaten and their clothes dry, Phainon leaned back on his hands, eyes raised to the stars. “I almost forgot how good fresh fish tastes.”

Mydei didn’t respond right away. He was still sitting upright, staring into the fire. He looked deep in thoughts, almost troubled.

Phainon glanced over and instantly noticed the shift. “What’s wrong?”

Mydei was silent for a bit longer, then he spoke quietly. “My father taught me to fish when I was young.”

Phainon straightened slightly. “Yeah?”

Mydei nodded slowly. “He wasn’t a kind man… but there were moments, before strife consumed him. I held onto hope for longer than I should have.”

“No one ever speaks of him.” Phainon pointed out. He had heard people talking about the queen, but no one ever mentioned the king.

Mydei’s voice remained calm. “I killed him.”

Phainon stayed quiet. What could he even say?

“He was going to destroy everything. Our people, our home, his own family. I had no choice.” Mydei continued.

It was the first time he’d spoken of it aloud since it happened. In Castrum Kremnos, everyone knew, but no one dared to ask. But Phainon deserved the truth. At least, so he could understand why Mydei revealed his own weak spot to him.

Phainon reached out, hesitating only briefly before placing a hand gently on Mydei’s arm. “You did what had to be done.”

“I will need you to do the same, should the time come,” Mydei whispered, looking into his eyes.

“I won’t let it come to that,” Phainon said, determined to be there for him.

Then Mydei leaned in, resting his forehead lightly against Phainon’s.

“Good,” he whispered. “That’s all I need.”

Soon, they reached Aedes Elysiae. The yellow wheat fields came into view, shining under the blinding sun. An old wooden fence surrounded the wheat fields and ended at the stone path that led to the village.

At the edge of the fence, a pink silhouette could be seen from far away. It hopped off the fence, approaching rapidly. Phainon knew exactly what it was, and without warning his travelling companion, he bolted.

Cyrene jumped into Phainon’s arms, hugging him like they hadn’t seen each other in years.

“Phainon! You’re finally home!”

“I missed you so much, Cyrene!”

“The nerve!” she exclaimed before looking up at him with a pout. “You made me think you were dead for two weeks. Two whole weeks!”

Phainon let go of her, rubbing the back of his neck. “Sorry… a lot happened during these two weeks. I swear I can explain!”

“You better,” she said, then looked behind Phainon to see Mydei standing a respectful distance away, probably to give them privacy.

“Is that your boyfriend?” she asked in a hushed tone.

“What? No!” Phainon’s face flushed red. “At least I don’t think so…”

Cyrene gasped at that, marching toward her soon to be brother in law.

“Hello! I’m Cyrene, Phainon’s friend!”

“I’m Mydeimos. It’s nice to finally meet you. Phainon talks a lot about you.”

“I hope only good things,” she replied with a chuckle.

“How about we walk and talk?” Phainon interjected.

As they walked, Phainon asked about home, his parents, and everyone else. Cyrene filled him in, mostly reassuring him that he could ask them himself once they arrived.

True to her word, the moment Phainon stepped through the front door, he was immediately enveloped in a tight hug by both of his parents.

“We missed you so much,” his mother whispered, her voice emotional.

His father gave him a firm pat on the back. “About time you came home, son.”

Phainon smiled, relieved to see his parents were looking well. “I missed you too.”

Then, as if just remembering, he turned slightly and gestured behind him. “Uh… I brought someone.”

Mydei stepped forward, offering a polite nod. “I’m Mydeimos. It’s an honor to meet you.”

Audata stepped forward, extending a hand. “Any friend of Phainon’s is welcome here. Don’t hesitate to ask if you need anything.”

“How about you two settle in and join us for lunch? Food is almost ready,” Hieronymus added with a smile.

Grateful for the warm welcome, they nodded and made their way down the hallway to Phainon’s room.

As soon as the door closed behind them, Phainon let out a breath he hadn’t realized he was holding. What was he even nervous about?

Mydei gave a small smile. “Your parents are kind. I see where you get it.”

Phainon laughed, flopping onto his bed. “They did raise me after all.”

Mydei glanced around the room, taking in the cluttered shelves, the faded pictures on the walls, and an old, rusty sword discarded near the corner. “It’s very... you.”

“Charming?” Phainon asked with a grin.

“I was going to say messy.” Mydei smirked and sat beside him on the bed, shooting him a sideways glance.

“I’m not messy…”

“Hm…” Mydei hummed thoughtfully. “Are we sharing your bed tonight?”

Phainon blinked, suddenly aware of how small the bed really was. “You could sleep on top of me?” he suggested, before realizing how that sounded.

“I’d crush you,” Mydei replied, rolling his eyes.

“Who says I wouldn’t like it?”

Mydei turned to him, eyebrow raised. “Careful. You keep saying things like that, and I might take you seriously.”

Phainon wrapped his arms around his neck, bringing him down. “Maybe I want you to.”

And that was all the permission Mydei needed.

He closed the distance, pressing his lips gently to Phainon’s. Phainon melted into it, one hand sliding down to rest against Mydei’s chest, the other still curled around his neck.

When they finally pulled apart, Mydei rested his forehead against Phainon’s.

“Well,” Phainon murmured, breathless. “That settles the bed question.”

Mydei chuckled. “We’ll figure it out after lunch.”

A knock at the door broke the moment.

“Guys! You're not making out in there, are you?” Cyrene called teasingly.

Phainon groaned, flopping back dramatically. “She’s the worst.”

Mydei smirked, standing and offering him a hand. “Come on.”

The table was already set when they arrived, the smell of roasted vegetables and freshly baked bread filling the air. Cyrene was already seated, grinning like a cat who knew exactly what she'd interrupted.

Phainon sat down, avoiding eye contact with her just as his mother and father entered, setting down the last of the dishes.

Once everyone was seated, conversation naturally shifted toward Phainon, about his trip to Castrum Kremnos, the brutal first days of training under Leonnius, and how he found himself helping out in Perdikkas’ infirmary.

His parents and Cyrene listened, occasionally asking questions or prompting for more detail. It felt good, being back home.

Then Cyrene turned to Mydei. “So… how did you two meet?”

The table quieted.

Phainon stiffened slightly. How exactly should he explain the ten day, ten night duel in a way that didn’t sound completely crazy?

Thankfully, Mydei answered smoothly. “We became sparring partners.”

“Is that so?” Cyrene tilted her head.

“Yes! I managed to beat two of Mydei’s generals trainings, so I was granted the honor of sparring with his majesty,” Phainon teased.

Everyone at the table froze.

“His Majesty?”

Right... he might have forgotten to mention one small detail about the friend he was bringing.

Mydei clicked his tongue, shooting Phainon a disapproving glance. “I told you not to call me by my title.”

“Mydei is a king?” Cyrene asked, eyes wide.

“A prince,” Phainon corrected.

Cyrene immediately grabbed Phainon by the sleeve and pulled him in to whisper-yell into his ear, “You brought a prince home and didn’t think that was worth mentioning ahead of time??”

“There’s no need to treat me any differently,” Mydei said, stepping in to defuse the moment. “Prince is only a title.”

“Yeah! Seriously I wouldn’t have known Mydei was the prince if Perdikkas hadn’t told me.” Phainon added.

“If you say so…” Audata muttered, glancing toward her husband. The two exchanged a look, visibly uneasy.

Noticing the tension lingering in the room, Phainon had a sudden, bright idea.

“Thank you for the amazing food! Mydei and I will wash the dishes so you all can rest,” he said quickly, already stacking empty plates.

“What? No, you-” Hieronymus began, but Mydei rose and followed after Phainon.

“It’s the least we can do,” he said, collecting the remaining dishes.

Audata looked like she wanted to protest, but stopped herself. “Well… alright then.”

In the kitchen, the clatter of dishes and running water filled the silence. Phainon rolled up his sleeves, glancing sideways at Mydei. They washed the dishes in silence, Phainon scrubbing and Mydei rinsing. That was until Phainon nudged Mydei with his hip.

“What?” He asked, glancing over.

“You’ve got something on your nose.”

Mydei frowned in confusion. Before he could react, Phainon grinned and reached out, gently pressing a finger to the tip of Mydei’s nose, leaving behind bubbles of soap.

Mydei looked unimpressed. “Very funny.”

Without warning, he leaned in and wiped his nose on Phainon’s shoulder.

“Hey!” Phainon protested, pulling back. “You’re getting my shirt dirty!”

“Is the great Phainon afraid of a little soap now?”

Phainon pouted, then dipped a finger back into the soapy water, forming a circle and blowing through it. A single bubble floated up, before popping directly in Mydei’s face. It burst against his eyes.

Soap didn’t faze him, he’d taken worse to the face in battle. But that didn’t mean he was going to let the little stunt slide. Without a word, he calmly rinsed a cup, filled it halfway with water, then turned and splashed it right at Phainon, who gasped as cold water hit his shirt and face.

Phainon scooped up a ball of bubbly soap, already dripping from his hands, and flung it at Mydei’s face.

But Mydei’s reflexes were sharper than expected, and he ducked.

The soap ball flew past him... and collided with the hair of a suddenly very angry Cyrene, who had just walked through the kitchen door.

“Phainon!” she shrieked, as she stomped toward him, bubbles clinging to her hair.

Phainon froze. “I’m sorry! It wasn’t supposed to hit you! I was aiming for-”

But she wasn’t listening.

“You ruined my hair!” she yelled, grabbing a dishtowel as if it were a weapon.

“How could you, Phainon?” Mydei asked, a smirk on his lips.

“You ducked!”

“And you threw it,” Cyrene said, closing in.

Phainon backed up slowly, hands raised in surrender. “I can help fix your-”

“You can fix your attitude!” she snapped, lunging at him with the towel.

Phainon yelped and ran for it, slipping slightly on the wet floor as Cyrene chased after him through the kitchen, shouting threats and wielding the towel like a weapon.

Mydei brought his attention back to the dishes, rinsing the few remaining cups, not bothering to land Phainon a hand.

Eventually, Cyrene cornered Phainon near the pantry and delivered a satisfying smack of towel to his arm.

“Ow! That’s abuse!” Phainon cried.

“That’s justice!” she declared, victorious.

Defeated, Phainon shuffled over to Mydei and rested his face against his shoulder. “You’re not going to defend me?”

“You had it coming,” Mydei said, shrugging him off. “Why don’t you go get changed while I finish the dishes?”

Phainon huffed but obeyed, muttering something about betrayal as he headed to his room. He took off his damp shirt, swapped it out for something dry, and ran a towel through his hair.

But when he returned, the kitchen was empty. The dishes were done, the counter wiped clean, and not a trace of Mydei or Cyrene in sight.

He wandered toward Cyrene’s room, and as it turned out, he found her sat cross-legged on her bed, while Mydei sat behind her, making small braids into her hair, similar to the one he made for himself. He attached cute bows at the end. The sight was adorable, and Phainon’s heart felt warm seeing his two favorite people getting along.

After Cyrene insisted on telling Mydei a series of increasingly embarrassing stories about Phainon, she was called away to help Audata with something in the kitchen.

It gave Phainon and Mydei a rare moment alone, just in time for the sunset.

“Come with me!” Phainon said, grabbing Mydei’s hand.

Without explanation, he led him through the back door and across the open fields until they reached the golden wheat fields they’d passed on their arrival.

Phainon guided him to a familiar spot, a small dip in the field where the wheat grew a little lighter, perfect for lying down without being completely swallowed by the crop.

They settled into the grass side by side, their shoulders just touching. Above them, the sky blazed with golden hues.

Phainon sighed contentedly. “Just in time.”

“It’s beautiful,” Mydei said, eyes fixed on the sky as the last streaks of gold faded into pink, then violet.

“I love it here,” Phainon murmured. “It’s calm. And when you lie down, no one can see you. It feels like the world forgets you for a while, and you finally get to breathe.”

Mydei nodded and reached for Phainon’s hand, intertwining their fingers as the night overtook.  After a few minutes of silence, Phainon glanced over, uncertainty in his expression. There was a question gnawing at him, and though the moment was quiet, the need to ask outweighed the risk of ruining it.

“Mydei… I’ve been wondering for a bit.” He paused, fingers tightening slightly around his. “What are we?” Because sitting in these wheat fields, laying so close together didn’t feel like just friends. Nor the kisses they shared.

Mydei turned his head toward him. “What are we?” he repeated. “We’re equals. Why do you ask?”

It was an honest answer, but not the one Phainon was looking for

“I just thought…” Phainon hesitated, gathering the courage to speak the truth sitting on his chest. “You and I have grown close since we first met. Really close. And it feels strange, wrong, even to just call you a friend. So I wanted to ask if you’d like to be more.”

He looked away after saying it, hoping his voice hadn’t sounded as shaky as he felt.

Mydei looked confused and asked, “Aren’t we already together?”

“What?”

“I thought we were,” Mydei said, sounding disappointed. “We’ve kissed, slept next to each other. I entrusted you with my secrets, my burdens. Was that not… being together?”

Phainon let out a sigh of relief. “I mean, yeah! That is what being together is. I guess I just… needed to hear you say it.”

Mydei gave a smile, his thumb brushing along the back of Phainon’s hand. “Then yes, Phainon. We’re together.”

Phainon leaned in closer, their foreheads touching. “Boyfriends?”

Mydei chuckled. He leaned in, pressing a gentle kiss to Phainon’s lips. “Yes. Boyfriends. If that’s what you want to call it.”

Their lips brushed again, lingering, like neither of them wanted to end the kiss, but the words between them still needed to be said.

Phainon pulled back slightly. “What do you call being together in Castrum Kremnos?”

Mydei paused for only a second before replying, “We call it marriage.”

Phainon’s eyes widened. “Seriously? Straight to marriage?”

“When you know you’ve found your kindred spirit,” Mydei said, lifting Phainon’s hand and placing a soft kiss to his knuckles, “marriage shouldn’t be a question. It’s just the next step.”

Phainon’s breath caught in his throat. Mydei looked sincere, and his gaze made Phainon’s stomach flip.

“And I’m certain,” Mydei continued, “that we are meant to be.”

For once, Phainon didn’t try to joke his way out of the fluttering in his chest. He simply stared at him, awestruck.

“I think I’m starting to believe that too.” Phainon said, voice trembling slightly.

Mydei pulled himself closer, resting his head on his boyfriend’s chest. “Good.”

They stayed there, under the shining stars. In that moment, nothing mattered more than each other.
